name: og-res-phosphorus-availability
title: The Phosphorus Bottleneck
question: Phosphorus may be a harder bottleneck than carbon. Can the same thermal-gradient vent pore that concentrates C and N also co-concentrate P — tracking dissolved phosphate, mineral-bound P, polyphosphate and reactive P with explicit precipitation/adsorption loss — or does phosphate precipitate/adsorb before it is chemically useful? Are there local windows where reactive P is produced faster than it is lost?
hypothesis: In a thermal-gradient pore (coupled from og-03), enrichment drives phosphate condensation and activation steeply enough that reactive-P formation outruns the first-order precipitation/adsorption sink in a bounded (source × enrichment) region — and that same enrichment co-concentrates P alongside carbon; without the gradient (open pore), precipitation wins and no reactive P accumulates.
objective: Build a real P-speciation process (phosphate <-> polyphosphate <-> reactive-P with a precipitation/adsorption mineral sink), couple it to the og-03 thermal pore, and map where reactive-P availability beats loss and co-concentrates with carbon.
result: All three gates pass — a favorable enriched pore produces reactive P faster than phosphate precipitates (net availability ~+1.8e-6 mol/s, only ~6% precipitated), the real og-03 thermophoretic pore co-concentrates P alongside carbon, and the open-pore / no-gradient ablation collapses reactive-P availability (net < 0, ~96% precipitated). P mass is conserved to ~5e-7.
claim: A real libRoadRunner P-speciation network coupled to the og-03 thermal pore shows reactive phosphorus becomes available only in a bounded (phosphate source × pore enrichment) window where condensation + activation outrun the precipitation/adsorption sink; the same pore enrichment that concentrates carbon co-concentrates P, and without the gradient phosphate precipitates before it is useful — phosphorus is a localization-gated bottleneck, not a free resource.

findings.statement: In the favorable thermal-gradient pore, reactive-P formation outpaces the precipitation/adsorption loss — net reactive-P availability settles positive (~+1.8e-6 mol/s) and reactive P accumulates to ~94% of the supplied phosphorus while only ~6% precipitates. A bounded local window exists where reactive P is produced faster than it is lost.

evidence.observed: ~+1.8e-6 mol/s net availability; reactive P ~94% of supply; ~6% precipitated

findings.explanation: Real libRoadRunner ODE P-speciation network: enrichment enters condensation as enr^2 and activation as enr, while precipitation is first-order in phosphate, so a concentrated pore tips phosphate's fate toward the reactive route.

findings.statement: The SAME real og-03 thermophoretic pore that lifts a dilute carbon feed across the ignition threshold (species-agnostic Soret + convection trap) co-concentrates phosphate: at the pore's enrichment the P reactive-availability is positive and the enrichment exceeds the carbon co-concentration floor (~10×). C and P co-concentrate in one pore regime — reported as an overlap boundary, not a fitted target.

evidence.observed: og-03 pore enrichment >> 10× carbon co-concentration floor; P reactive-availability positive at that enrichment

findings.explanation: The thermophoretic trap enrichment depends on the Soret coefficient and pore geometry, not on the solute identity, so the pore that concentrates carbon concentrates phosphate; coupling it to the P-speciation network shows reactive P becomes available in the same regime.

findings.statement: The feature ablation is decisive — an open pore / no thermal gradient (enrichment = 1) collapses reactive-P availability: net availability goes negative and ~96% of phosphorus precipitates to the mineral sink. Phosphate precipitates/adsorbs before it is chemically useful unless the pore concentrates it first.

evidence.observed: favorable net ~+1.8e-6 (6% precipitated) vs open-pore net < 0 (~96% precipitated)

findings.explanation: Without enrichment the condensation/activation fluxes (enr-gated) fall below the first-order precipitation loss, so phosphate drains into mineral-bound P — the phosphorus bottleneck made explicit.

findings.statement: A 16×16 sweep over (phosphate source × pore/thermal enrichment) maps where reactive P is available, not just that it is at one point. Reactive-P availability is bounded by the net-availability threshold (production = loss) on the enrichment axis; the PASS region is where that threshold is crossed AND the enrichment co-concentrates carbon (right of the ~10× carbon floor). Below the threshold phosphate precipitates before it is useful.

evidence.observed: reactive-P pool ranges ~0 to ~1 mM across the (source × enrichment) plane (~94% of supply, ~94 µM, at the favorable 1e-4 M point); availability bounded by net=0 and the carbon co-concentration floor

findings.explanation: 16×16 sweep of the real libRoadRunner composite reduced to the settled reactive-P pool, net availability and precipitated fraction; rendered as the reactive-P availability phase map (Decision view). Runner sims/compute_phosphorus_availability_grid.py.

report.title: The phosphorus bottleneck — reactive-P availability + co-concentration
report.verdict: PASS — reactive P is available in a bounded enriched-pore window that co-concentrates with carbon
report.main_insight: Phosphorus is a localization-gated bottleneck: reactive P becomes available only where a thermal pore concentrates phosphate faster than it precipitates, and the same pore that concentrates carbon co-concentrates P — without the gradient, phosphate precipitates before it is useful.
report.conclusion: A real P-speciation network coupled to the og-03 thermal pore reproduces the phosphorus bottleneck and locates the window where reactive P wins the race against precipitation, co-concentrating with carbon.
report.caveat: The speciation kinetics are a lumped, provenance-carrying reduced network (one reactive-P pool, a reversible mineral sink); absolute rate constants are calibrated to give the precipitation-vs-reactive competition, not fit to a specific mineral assemblage.

conclusion: Reactive phosphorus becomes available only in a bounded enriched-pore window where condensation and activation outrun the precipitation/adsorption sink; the same og-03 pore co-concentrates P with carbon, and the open-pore ablation precipitates ~96% of P — phosphorus is a localization-gated bottleneck.

biological_validation.basis: Reactive-P availability beats loss in the favorable pore and co-concentrates with carbon, with the open-pore ablation collapsing it.

explanatory_gain.basis: The real speciation network shows WHY P is a harder bottleneck — precipitation is first-order while the useful routes are enrichment-gated, so P needs localization that C needs less.

limitations: The P-speciation network is a lumped reduced model (single reactive-P pool, reversible mineral sink); rate constants are calibrated to the precipitation-vs-reactive competition, not fit to a mineral assemblage.
The co-concentration argument uses the og-03 trap enrichment as a species-agnostic multiplier into the P network; a fully coupled spatial C+P pore solve is deferred.
natcomm2023phosphorus / natcomm2025phosphateactivation (plan refs) are not yet on main's papers.bib — recorded as pending proposed_inputs, not cited here.

resolved_uncertainties: A bounded (source × enrichment) window exists where reactive P is produced faster than it precipitates.
The same thermal pore that concentrates carbon co-concentrates phosphorus.
remaining_uncertainties: Whether a fully coupled spatial C+N+P pore solve preserves the co-concentration overlap under shared transport.
